title: Learn the Signs. Act Early. Milestone checklists, 2 months to 5 years
publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention with the American Academy of Pediatrics
note: Each checklist lists milestones that most children (75% or more) reach by that age, so a missing milestone is a prompt to talk to a professional rather than a sign of being behind average. Public domain.

title: Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools (Zubler JM, Wiggins LD, Macias MM, et al.)
note: The evidence review behind the 2022 CDC/AAP checklists: an expert working group chose milestones from published normative data; about 80% of final milestones had normative data from multiple sources. Social-emotional and cognitive milestones had the least normative data.

title: WHO Motor Development Study: windows of achievement for six gross motor development milestones (Martorell R, de Onis M, et al.)
publisher: Acta Paediatrica 95(S450):86-95, WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study
note: Longitudinal data from healthy children in Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the USA. Windows run from the 1st to the 99th percentile. 4.3% of children never crawled on hands and knees.

title: Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age
note: Infants: floor-based play several times a day, at least 30 minutes of tummy time spread through the day for those not yet mobile, no screen time, not restrained for more than an hour at a time. Sleep 14-17 hours (0-3 months), 12-16 hours (4-11 months), 11-14 hours (1-2 years), 10-13 hours (3-4 years). Screen time not recommended under 2; no more than 1 hour a day at 2-4 years.

title: Tummy time and infant health outcomes: a systematic review (Hewitt L, Kerr E, Stanley RM, Okely AD)
note: 16 studies, 4,237 infants: tummy time was positively associated with gross motor and total development and with preventing brachycephaly (flat head).

title: Beyond the 30-million-word gap: children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function (Romeo RR, et al.)
note: Back-and-forth conversational turns with adults, more than the number of words heard, were linked to children's language skills and language-related brain activity.

title: Literacy promotion: an essential component of primary care pediatric practice. Policy statement (Klass P, Miller-Fitzwater A, High PC)
note: Recommends shared reading from birth; the accompanying technical report reviews evidence that it supports language, cognitive and social-emotional development.

title: Sleep-related infant deaths: updated 2022 recommendations for reducing infant deaths in the sleep environment (Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I)

title: Randomized trial of peanut consumption in infants at risk for peanut allergy (LEAP; Du Toit G, et al.)
note: Early introduction of peanut lowered peanut allergy in high-risk infants. Babies with severe eczema or a known allergy should get advice before introducing peanut.

note: Good sources of iron include red meat, beans such as kidney beans, edamame and chickpeas, nuts, dried fruit and fortified breakfast cereals.

Early introduction of food allergens
publisher: British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology
note: Introduce egg and peanut in age-appropriate forms from around 6 months, and before 1 year. Babies with a food allergy or severe eczema need professional advice first.

title: Randomized trial of introduction of allergenic foods in breast-fed infants (EAT; Perkin MR, et al.)
note: No significant difference overall, but among infants who ate enough of the six allergenic foods regularly, egg and peanut allergy were less common.

title: Development and pilot testing of Baby-Led Introduction to SolidS (Cameron SL, Taylor RW, Heath AM)
note: The BLISS version of baby-led weaning: food babies can feed themselves, a high-iron and a high-energy food at each meal, food soft enough to squash with the tongue, and a list of high-choking-risk foods to avoid.

title: A baby-led approach to eating solids and risk of choking (Fangupo LJ, et al.)
note: Randomised trial of 206 babies: those following BLISS did not choke more often than spoon-fed babies; about a third of babies in both groups choked at least once between 6 and 8 months.

title: Effects of repeated exposure on acceptance of initially disliked vegetables in 7-month old infants (Maier A, et al.)
note: Intake of a disliked vegetable rose to match a liked one by about the 8th offering, and most infants still ate it 9 months later.

title: Effects of repeated exposure to either vegetables or fruits on infant's vegetable and fruit acceptance at the beginning of weaning (Barends C, et al.)
note: Starting weaning with vegetables, not fruit, increased vegetable acceptance.

title: Childcare and early years education (Best Start in Life)
note: 15 and 30 hours support for children aged 9 months to 4 years, Tax-Free Childcare and the Childcare Checker.

title: Apply for a primary school place
note: Apply through your local council, even for schools in another council area.

title: National Offer Day (primary)
note: England's national timetable: applications close on 15 January and primary offers are made on 16 April, or the next working day.

title: WHO Child Growth Standards: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age and head circumference-for-age (expanded tables)
note: How healthy breastfed children grow from birth to 5 years in good conditions, measured in six countries. Used here under CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO.

title: UK-WHO growth charts, 0-4 years
publisher: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health
note: The UK charts in the red book use the WHO standards from 2 weeks to 4 years, with nine centile lines two thirds of a standard deviation apart, and correct for gestation when babies are born before 37 weeks.

title: Faltering growth: recognition and management (NG75)
publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
note: Concern thresholds: weight falling across 1 or more centile spaces if birthweight was below the 9th centile, 2 or more if between the 9th and 91st, 3 or more if above the 91st, or current weight below the 2nd centile.

title: Baby teething symptoms
note: Front teeth around 6 months, then lateral incisors (8), first molars (12), canines (18) and second molars (24); bottom teeth usually first; all milk teeth by 2 to 3 years.
